title: Wound dressing change
what: A nurse or doctor takes off the old dressing, cleans the wound, and puts on a new one. This helps the wound heal cleaner and faster.
why: After surgery, and for cuts, burns, scrapes, stitches, and other wounds.
tell_doctor: If you are allergic to antiseptics, iodine, or medical tape
If you have diabetes. Wounds heal more slowly
If the wound hurts more or is leaking fluid

prepare.title: Dressing
prepare.text: Do not take the dressing off yourself unless your doctor said you can. Keep it dry.

prepare.title: Pain
prepare.text: If dressing changes usually hurt, ask your doctor ahead of time about pain relief.

prepare.title: Clothes
prepare.text: Wear loose clothes so the wound is easy to reach.

bring: Your discharge papers or your doctor's orders
Your own dressing supplies, if you were asked to bring them
steps: You sit or lie down so the wound is easy to reach
The old dressing is gently removed. If it is stuck, it is soaked with a solution first
The nurse or doctor checks the wound
The wound and the skin around it are cleaned with antiseptic
A new sterile dressing is put on and secured
feel: The antiseptic may sting a little
Removing a stuck dressing can be unpleasant. Say so if it hurts
after: Keep the dressing clean and dry
The next change depends on how the wound looks, often in 1 to 3 days
Before you shower, ask if the dressing can get wet
red_flags: The dressing quickly soaks through with blood
The wound is red, swollen, or hot, or has pus or a bad smell

faq.q: How often should a dressing be changed?
faq.a: It varies, from every day to once every few days. The doctor will tell you after looking at the wound.

faq.q: Can I change my dressing at home?
faq.a: Simple dressings are often changed at home once the doctor shows you how. Complex wounds are best done at the clinic.
